claims.text: Inventory is the stock of goods a business holds at a point in time. It has three types: the raw materials and components it has bought but not yet used, the work in progress that has entered its process but is not yet finished, and the finished products it has made but not yet sold.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Raw materials inventory is held because supply arrives in batches while production consumes material continuously: a stock of inputs keeps the process running between deliveries, and it keeps it running when a delivery is late or usage is heavier than planned.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Some work in progress is unavoidable, because any process that takes time has partly finished output inside it at any moment. A business may also hold more than that minimum on purpose, placing a small stock between two stages so that the later stage can keep working for a while when the earlier one stops.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Finished-product inventory lets a business supply a customer immediately instead of waiting for a production run, and lets it produce at a steady rate while sales rise and fall through the year. A service business holds materials and consumables but cannot hold a finished service, because a service is produced at the moment it is consumed.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The cost of holding inventory has four parts: space and its running (rent or the value of space the business owns, refrigeration, security, insurance and handling labour); the capital tied up in goods that are not yet earning anything; what can happen to goods while they wait, which is deterioration, obsolescence, damage and theft; and the administrative cost of ordering and record-keeping.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A business usually estimates what inventory costs it to hold as a rate applied to the value held: annual holding cost = average inventory value x holding-cost rate. The rate is an estimate that bundles storage, capital and risk into one percentage.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Holding inventory buys four things: demand that arrives unexpectedly can be met from stock, production continues when a delivery is late, larger orders may earn a bulk discount and spread delivery charges over more units, and output can be produced at a steady rate while sales vary.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Running out of inventory has a cost that no invoice records: production stops or an order goes unfilled, so the contribution on the lost sales is lost, the fixed costs of the period are incurred anyway, and a customer who is turned away may buy elsewhere next time as well.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The amount of inventory worth holding is the level at which holding more stops being cheaper than the stock-outs that more would prevent. Because both sides are made of the business's own figures - its holding-cost rate, its contribution per unit and how reliable its supply is - the right level differs between businesses and moves when those figures move.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Lead time is the time between placing an order with a supplier and the goods being available to use. It includes the supplier's own processing, transport, customs clearance on imported goods and the buyer's goods-inwards checking, and in practice it is described by two figures: how long it usually takes and how much it varies.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Buffer inventory, also called safety stock or the minimum inventory level, is the quantity a business plans to hold in reserve above what it expects to use during the lead time, so that usage heavier than expected or a delivery later than promised does not stop it working.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The re-order level is the inventory level at which the next order is placed, and it is calculated as re-order level = (average usage per day x lead time in days) + buffer inventory. The first part covers what will be used while the order is on its way; the second is the reserve that should still be untouched when the delivery arrives.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The re-order quantity is a separate decision from the re-order level: it is how much is ordered each time. Where deliveries arrive just as the buffer is reached, the maximum inventory level is the buffer inventory plus the re-order quantity, and the average level is roughly the buffer plus half the re-order quantity.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A longer lead time raises the usage that has to be covered while an order travels, and a lead time that varies more raises the buffer needed for the same protection. Both raise the re-order level, the average inventory held and therefore the holding cost, without any change in what the business sells.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A simple inventory control chart plots the inventory level on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal axis. The plotted line falls as inventory is used and rises vertically when a delivery arrives, giving a saw-tooth shape, and horizontal lines are drawn across it at the maximum inventory level, the re-order level and the buffer inventory level.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Four quantities can be read from a simple inventory control chart: the usage rate from the steepness of the falling line, the lead time from the horizontal distance between the point where the line crosses the re-order level and the vertical rise that follows, the re-order quantity from the height of that rise, and whether the buffer was broken into from whether the line went below the buffer inventory line.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A falling line steeper than planned means inventory is being used faster than assumed, so the re-order level and the buffer are reached earlier than intended. A rise plotted further to the right than the planned lead time means the supplier was late, and the extra fall comes out of the buffer. If either goes far enough the line reaches zero, which is a stock-out.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The saw-tooth shape assumes steady usage and constant-sized deliveries arriving on time, and real usage and real deliveries vary, so an inventory control chart is a plan the actual line is compared against rather than a forecast of what will happen. It also tracks one item and shows quantity rather than value, so it says nothing on its own about how much capital is standing still.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Supply chain management is the management of the flow of materials, information and money along the whole chain from the original suppliers, through the business's own operations, to the final customer and back again for returns. For one business it covers choosing and managing suppliers, purchasing, inbound transport, inventory, production scheduling, warehousing and delivery to the customer.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: What a business can promise its customers depends on parts of the chain it does not own: a supplier's delay becomes its delay because the order cannot be completed without the part, a supplier's defect reaches the customer under its own name, and cost added anywhere in the chain ends up either in the price the customer pays or in the margin the business keeps.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Where supply chain management shortens the lead time and makes it more predictable, the buffer inventory needed for the same protection falls, releasing capital and lowering holding cost. How large that saving is depends on how much of the inventory was there to cover lead-time uncertainty rather than to earn bulk discounts.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Much of what Namibian businesses use is imported through Walvis Bay or brought overland from South Africa, so inbound lead times are long and can vary with port handling, border formalities and road transport. Long and variable lead times raise both the usage that must be covered while an order travels and the buffer on top of it, so supply arrangements carry more weight for inventory here than distance alone suggests.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Just in time (JIT) is an approach to inventory in which materials and components are ordered and delivered so that they arrive as they are needed in production, and output is made to fill orders rather than to build a stock of finished products, so that very little inventory is held at any stage.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Just in case (JIC) is an approach to inventory in which a business deliberately holds buffer stocks of materials and finished products so that production and sales can continue when a delivery is late, a machine fails or demand is higher than expected.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The purpose of JIT is to remove the cost of holding inventory, to release the capital and the space that inventory occupies, and to make problems visible: with no reserve to draw on, a defective batch or an unreliable machine stops the process at once instead of being absorbed quietly.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The purpose of JIC is continuity. The inventory is insurance, so that a disruption upstream or a jump in demand does not halt production or lose a sale, and the price paid for that insurance is the holding cost.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: JIT depends on conditions being in place: suppliers that deliver small quantities reliably and often, dependable transport, demand information shared far enough ahead for a supplier to plan, quality good enough that a defective part does not halt the process, a workforce able to move between tasks, and ordering systems that can carry many small orders. Where those conditions are weak, the same approach that removes holding cost exposes the business to stoppages.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Adopting JIT lowers the average value of inventory held, so the annual holding cost falls with it and the capital released becomes available for other uses. The size of both effects is set by how much inventory value is removed and by the business's own holding-cost rate, so it has to be calculated for the particular business rather than assumed.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Smaller, more frequent deliveries raise the number of deliveries paid for and may lose quantity discounts, so part of the holding-cost saving is given back. Whether JIT lowers total cost depends on comparing the two amounts, and the comparison can come out either way.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Under JIT an interruption to supply reaches production quickly because there is little inventory to absorb it, so a delay that a buffer would have hidden can halt output. The cost is the contribution on the output not made, plus the fixed costs incurred during the stoppage, plus any penalty or lost order.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: JIT changes relationships as well as stock levels: it tends to mean fewer suppliers on longer agreements with shared schedules, staff trained to check quality at their own stage and to move between tasks, and customers who may get more choice but may also have to wait for made-to-order output.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Whether JIT suits a business depends on how near and how dependable its suppliers are, how steady its demand is, how large the holding cost it would save is against the cost of a stoppage, and whether its quality is good enough that one defect does not halt the process. Many businesses therefore apply it item by item rather than across the whole store.

verification.method: Authored 2026-09-12 under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic 4.2 contract and the 9609 v2 syllabus scope. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
